newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Summit lays foundations for new EU treaty - Spring.
newsitem.headline: Summit lays foundations for new EU treaty - Spring.

text.p: The Dublin summit of European Union leaders will demonstrate a new resolve in the fight against crime and unemployment and lay the foundations for a new EU treaty in 1997, Ireland's foreign minister said on Thursday.

Dick Spring said Ireland's six-month presidency of the EU had aimed to co-ordinate efforts to tackle drugs and crime, promote employment, prepare for a single currency and guide the bloc towards a new treaty to take it into the 21st century.

He said the two-day summit, which begins on Friday, would show progress had been made in all these areas, taking the bloc closer to the adoption of a new treaty at the end of the Netherlands's tenure of the presidency in June 1997.

"We posed ourselves several ambitious but realistic challenges in key areas relevant to the concerns of people in Europe in 1996," Spring said. "We believe we have realised our ambitions in all areas."

Spring said good progress had been made on a new EU treaty, with a draft treaty prepared covering all areas except contentious issues like the institutions of an enlarged Union and whether some countries should be able to integrate faster than others.
"We have produced a very readable and accessible document," he said. "The level of ambition is such that we want to have agreement and conclusions by June 1997 in Amsterdam."
But Spring said work was still needed to get the EU's 15 members to agree on a new treaty.

"Any fair and reasonable commentator would assess that the work done has been a major step forward in terms of arriving at conclusions in Amsterdam," he said. "But that is not to underestimate the scale of the challenge. It is going to require a great deal of work."

Spring said Ireland had made drugs and crime a particular priority. "In relation to drugs and crime we have made significant progress -- we have ensured that these issues are at the heart of the European agenda," he said.
"There was always lip-service and acknowledgement of the seriousness of these issues, but we have ensured measures are in place for working together in a co-ordinated reponse."

He said Britain -- one of the EU's less enthusiastic members -- was not expected to hold up the business of the Dublin summit, despite continuing divisions within the ruling Conservative Party over Europe.
"They have internal difficulties but I don't think that should affect their contribution to the meeting this weekend," Spring said. "Britain has alreay outlined its position on most issues."
